title: UNION & UNION ALL
description: Combine result sets vertically with UNION and UNION ALL, eliminate sorting overhead, and align column types.

data.text: Set operations combine rows from two or more queries vertically into a single result set. `UNION` merges results and removes duplicate rows, while `UNION ALL` concatenates all rows without deduplication.
UNION vs UNION ALL: Performance Difference

rows: High: Requires sorting or building an in-memory hash table
Use only when duplicate removal is strictly necessary
Recommended default choice for combining datasets

data.title: Combining Active and Archived Messages with UNION ALL
data.code:
SELECT id, user_id, content, created_at, 'active' AS source
FROM active_messages
WHERE user_id = $1

UNION ALL

SELECT id, user_id, content, created_at, 'archive' AS source
FROM archived_messages
WHERE user_id = $1
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 50;

data.text: Aligning Columns and Ordering the Result

UNION requires the same number of columns in the same order with compatible types. If the types differ, PostgreSQL tries to find a common type and can fail with an error such as `UNION types text and integer cannot be matched`. The column names come from the first SELECT, and a single ORDER BY at the end sorts the combined result.

data.title: Combining sources with an aligned projection
data.content: Both branches return the same three columns with matching types, and the ORDER BY applies to the combined result.
data.code:
SELECT id, 'active' AS source, created_at AS event_at
FROM active_users

UNION ALL

SELECT id, 'archived' AS source, created_at AS event_at
FROM archived_users

ORDER BY event_at DESC
LIMIT 100;

data.title: When UNION and JOIN solve different problems
data.text: UNION stacks rows vertically; JOIN adds columns horizontally. If two tables have the same shape and you want one combined list, use UNION. If two tables describe the same entity and you want a wider row, use JOIN. Mixing those up is a common interview trap, so state which axis you are combining before you write the query.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: `UNION` removes duplicates; `UNION ALL` preserves all rows.
Always default to `UNION ALL` unless duplicate elimination is explicitly required.
Both subqueries must return the same number of columns with compatible data types.
